title: The IT Crowd: have you tried turning it off and on again?
description: Reynholm Industries' basement IT department ran for four series on Channel 4 and gave every support desk its motto. Questions cover the characters, the running jokes and the awards. Then the Quiz takes the motto seriously: why does turning it off and on again actually fix things, and why doesn't every "off" count?
author: Quizbun

questions.title: Roy picks up the phone in the IT department. What does he ask the caller, over and over, across the series?

options.text: "Have you tried turning it off and on again?"
"Have you tried clearing your cache?"
"What's your ticket number?"
"Have you read the manual?"

questions.explanation:
Roy asks it in the first episode, "Yesterday's Jam" (2006), and keeps asking it for the rest of the run. It works as a joke because it works as advice. Real help desks start with a restart because it fixes a large share of problems for almost no effort, and it rules out the easy causes before anyone spends time on the hard ones.

The last two Questions in this Quiz explain why it works.
questions.references: [Wikipedia: The IT Crowd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_IT_Crowd), [Wikipedia: List of The IT Crowd episodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_IT_Crowd_episodes)

questions.title: In "Calamity Jen", a TV advert announces the new emergency services number with a jingle. Type the number.
questions.description: Type the digits as one block or in the groups the jingle sings.
questions.explanation:
The number is **0118 999 881 999 119 725 3**, twenty digits, with a long pause before the final 3. Moss watches the advert and says it's easy to remember. Later in the same episode he sets the office on fire and reports it by email instead of phoning anyone.

The joke works because an emergency number has one hard requirement: someone in a panic, maybe in the dark or in smoke, has to dial it without thinking. That's why real emergency numbers are three digits long. The "0118" also echoes a real change: in 2003 the UK replaced its directory enquiries number, 192, with a crowd of commercial 118 numbers.

questions.title: Which of these numbers reach the police, fire and ambulance services from a phone in the UK?
questions.explanation:
**999** and **112** both reach the emergency services, and neither has priority. 112 is the pan-European emergency number. The UK added it in April 1995, and it connects to the same circuits as 999, which helps visitors who don't know the local number.

The others are real numbers with other jobs. 111 is the NHS line for urgent medical questions that aren't emergencies, 101 is the police non-emergency line, and 118 118 is one of the commercial directory enquiries services that the show's "0118" echoes.

questions.title: 999 is the oldest emergency telephone number in the world. In what year did it start in London?
questions.description: Enter a four-digit year. Answers within two years count.
questions.explanation:
999 started in the London area on **30 June 1937**. Its design is a lesson in usability for an emergency. Phones then had rotary dials, and 9 sits one hole from the finger stop, so a caller in darkness or smoke could find it by touch: put a finger in the last hole and turn the dial fully, three times. Payphones of the time could also be modified cheaply to let the 9 through without a coin.

The IT Crowd's twenty-digit number fails every one of those tests.

questions.title: The IT department sits in the basement of which company?

options.text: Reynholm Industries
Wernham Hogg
Initech
Pied Piper

questions.explanation:
The show is set at Reynholm Industries, 123 Carenden Road in central London. Its founder and chief executive is Denholm Reynholm (Chris Morris), who is later replaced by his son Douglas (Matt Berry).

The other three are fictional companies from other workplace comedies: Wernham Hogg from the British *The Office*, Initech from the film *Office Space*, and Pied Piper from *Silicon Valley*.

questions.title: Jen Barber is hired to run the IT department. What does she know about computers?

options.text: Almost nothing: her CV claimed a lot of experience with computers, and her interviewer knew even less
She is a former systems administrator promoted into management
She built Reynholm Industries' first network
She is a programmer who refuses to answer the phone

questions.explanation:
Jen (Katherine Parkinson) claims on her CV to have "a lot of experience with computers". Denholm doesn't know enough to test the claim, so her bluffing in the interview gets her the job of department head, which the show also calls relationship manager. Her real job becomes translating between the technicians and the rest of the building.

That is a real role. Many support teams have someone whose value is explaining problems to non-technical staff and managing expectations, even if they can't fix a printer themselves.

questions.title: Richmond Avenal (Noel Fielding) is kept in the server room. Why was he sent there?

options.text: He became a goth
He crashed the company's email system
He is the only person who can repair the servers
He was hired as a security guard for the servers

questions.explanation:
Richmond was once an up-and-coming executive at Reynholm Industries. When he became a goth, he was banished to the server room, out of sight of the rest of the company.

The joke is that the server room is where a company hides things it would rather forget. Real server rooms are loud and cold, because they're built for the machines' comfort, not people's: fans push air through the racks, and cooling keeps the hardware in its safe temperature range.

questions.title: In 2007 NBC filmed an American pilot of the show. Which member of the British cast played the same role in it?

options.text: Richard Ayoade
Chris O'Dowd
Katherine Parkinson
Chris Morris

questions.explanation:
Richard Ayoade played Moss in both versions. The rest of the American cast was new: Joel McHale as Roy, Jessica St. Clair as Jen and Rocky Carroll as Denholm. NBC announced a series for 2007–08, but the show never aired. The pilot leaked online in 2012.

Chris O'Dowd played Roy in the British version, Katherine Parkinson played Jen, and Chris Morris played Denholm. None of them appeared in the American pilot.

questions.title: In the Series 3 episode "Friendface", Jen persuades Roy and Moss to join Friendface. What is it a parody of?

options.text: Social networking sites such as Facebook
Video-sharing sites such as YouTube
Search engines such as Google
Webmail services such as Hotmail

questions.explanation:
Friendface is a social network, and its name is an obvious echo of Facebook. The episode aired on 19 December 2008, when Facebook had opened to everyone only two years earlier and joining one was still a new, slightly embarrassing thing to do.

The joke still lands because the business model hasn't changed: a social network grows by pulling people you know, or used to know, back into your life, whether or not you wanted them there.

questions.title: What did The IT Crowd win in 2008?

options.text: The International Emmy Award for comedy
The Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Comedy Series
The Golden Globe for Best Television Series, Musical or Comedy
Nothing; it won its first award after the final episode in 2013

questions.explanation:
The show won the **International Emmy** for comedy in 2008. The International Emmys are a separate set of awards for television made outside the United States, which is why a Channel 4 sitcom could win one. The Primetime Emmys, the ones for American shows, don't cover it.

The British awards followed. It won the BAFTA for Best Situation Comedy in 2009, and in 2014 Katherine Parkinson and Richard Ayoade won the BAFTAs for best female and male comedy performance.
questions.references: [Wikipedia: The IT Crowd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_IT_Crowd), [Wikipedia: International Emmy Award for Best Comedy Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Emmy_Award_for_Best_Comedy_Series)

questions.title: Counting only the four regular series, how many episodes of The IT Crowd are there?
questions.explanation:
There are **24**: four series of six episodes each, from 2006 to 2010. Short series are normal for British sitcoms, which are often written by one or two people; The IT Crowd had a single writer. An American network comedy of the same era usually ran for more than 20 episodes a season, written by a room of writers.

One more episode came later. "The Internet Is Coming", a 48-minute special, aired on 27 September 2013 and ended the show, making 25 in total.

questions.title: Which of these lines are from The IT Crowd?

options.text: "Have you tried turning it off and on again?"
"Did you see that ludicrous display last night?"
"Dear Sir stroke Madam, I am writing to inform you of a fire…"
"Bazinga!"
"I'm not superstitious, but I am a little stitious."

questions.explanation:
Three are real. Roy's catchphrase runs through the whole series. "Did you see that ludicrous display last night?" comes from "Are We Not Men?" (Series 3), where Roy and Moss memorise football small talk from a website so they can pass as fans; the reply is a complaint about Arsenal's Wenger bringing on Walcott too early. Moss starts his fire email in "Calamity Jen" with "Dear Sir stroke Madam", decides it's too formal, and rewrites it as "Fire, exclamation mark".

The other two come from American sitcoms: "Bazinga!" is Sheldon's catchphrase in *The Big Bang Theory*, and the "stitious" line is Michael Scott's in the American *The Office*.

questions.title: Why does turning a computer off and on again fix so many problems?

options.text: It throws away state that has built up: leaked memory, stuck processes, stale connections and caches
It installs any pending software updates
It cools the processor enough to stop calculation errors
It resets the hardware clock, which drifts over time

questions.explanation:
A running computer keeps a lot of state in memory: open files, network connections, caches, locks and the internal flags of every program. Bugs corrupt that state a little at a time. A program that forgets to free memory, a **memory leak**, uses a bit more each hour. A process waiting for a lock that never gets released sits there forever. A network connection whose other end has gone away still looks open.

A restart throws all of that away and rebuilds every program's state from its starting point, which was tested far more than day 40 of uptime was. The chart shows the catch: the bug is still in the code, so the problems build up again. Engineers call this **software aging**. Some systems schedule regular restarts on purpose, a practice called software rejuvenation.

Installing updates is a side effect some restarts carry, not the reason a restart fixes a frozen program. A reboot doesn't cool the processor in any useful way, and it doesn't reset the real-time clock, which runs on a battery precisely so that it survives a restart.

images.alt: Line chart of memory in use over days of uptime. From a clean start the line climbs steadily as leaks and stuck state pile up. At each reboot it drops straight back to the starting level, then climbs again along the same slope. A dashed line near the top marks all memory used, labelled swapping, freezes and crashes. After the last reboot the line is climbing towards it again, labelled same bug, same climb.
images.caption: Illustrative, not measured data. Chart: Quizbun.

questions.references: [Wikipedia: Software aging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_aging), [Wikipedia: Memory leak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_leak). Real systems that crashed after running too long are in the Quiz "Have you tried turning it off and on again? Real bugs a reboot hides".

questions.title: On a Windows 10 or 11 PC with default settings, which gives you a completely fresh Windows kernel?

options.text: Restart
Shut down, then press the power button
Both give an equally fresh start
Neither; only unplugging the power cable does

questions.explanation:
Since Windows 8, **Fast Startup** has been on by default. When you choose Shut down, Windows closes your apps and logs you off, but it doesn't close the kernel session. It saves the kernel and loaded drivers to the hibernation file, `hiberfil.sys`, and loads them back at the next power-on. That makes startup faster, but any bad state in the kernel or a driver comes back with it.

Microsoft's documentation says Fast Startup doesn't apply to Restart. A restart runs the full boot cycle, because people restart when they want a completely new Windows state. So when the help desk says "turn it off and on again" on a modern Windows PC, Restart is the button that does it.

Try it now: if your PC has been shut down every night for weeks and still feels sluggish, use Restart instead.
questions.references: [Microsoft Learn: Fast startup causes hibernation or shutdown to fail](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/windows-client/setup-upgrade-and-drivers/fast-startup-causes-system-hibernation-shutdown-fail), [Microsoft Learn: Distinguishing fast startup from wake-from-hibernation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/drivers/kernel/distinguishing-fast-startup-from-wake-from-hibernation)
